newsitem.title: USA: Stocks jump, Wall Street in election comfort zone.
newsitem.headline: Stocks jump, Wall Street in election comfort zone.

text.p: Stocks were broadly higher Tuesday as investors cheered the prospect that the Democrats will not re-take control of Congress in the national elections.

At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 43.60 points at 6,085.28 after a late morning rally of more than 50 points to 6,093.48 put in within flirting distance of its record closing high of 6,094.23 set on Oct. 18.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 14-8 on active volume of 280 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 10.12 points at 1,230.60. The American Stock Exchange index was up 1.48 at 573.24.

Wall Street had already accepted the likelihood of President Clinton's re-election but worries that he would enter his second term with a Democratic Congress had weighed on markets, which feared increased federal spending, resulting in deeper deficits and higher interest rates.

"The fear we would be taking a different course away from lower deficits, lower inflation and subdued economic growth is flying out the window," said Richard Cripps, vice president and chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
Wall Street appears to be favouring a split in government with Clinton in the White House and Republicans controlling Congress.

The reason is based on the belief that Democrats unchecked would run deep spending-driven deficits while Republicans unchecked would run equally deep deficits by failing to find spending cuts to pay for their tax cuts.
Instead, the odds favour a government that closely resembles the one now expiring, sustaining a political picture that so far has proven profitable for investors.
"It looks like Republicans will win Congress and that will keep the status quo, an environment Wall Street can live with," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross.
Clear evidence of Wall Street's confidence came from the bond market.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up nearly a full point, which lowered its yield to 6.58 percent -- the lowest since March 26 -- from 6.66 percent at Monday's close.
Politics from outside the United States also played a major part in the activity in at least one individual issue.
The Templeton Russia Fund climbed 1-1/4 to 21-3/4 after Russian President Boris Yeltsin's seven-hour heart bypass operation.
